title: Ninety-five theses (1517)
hook: Luther posts theses for debate, and printers carry them across Europe

segments.voice: Yesterday, Habakkuk's line in Romans, and a frightened monk who felt the gates open. Your line was the gates opened.

Hammer, nail, church door. That's the picture on posters, in films, on coffee mugs: a monk in a black habit nailing a sheet of paper to a wooden door while a crowd gasps. The story goes that Martin Luther did exactly that, at the castle church in Wittenberg, on the eve of All Saints. Historians still argue about the hammer. What isn't in doubt is the paper. It was written in Latin, in numbered points, and its title called it a disputation: an invitation to argue.

A thesis, in a university then, was a statement put up for debate. Scholars would post a list, and anyone could come and argue the other side. So Luther's theses weren't a manifesto. They were questions, sharpened into claims, about the indulgence preaching from two days ago. Luther preached in his town as well as teaching, and people from that town were coming back with indulgence letters and asking whether they still needed to change their lives. The very first thesis goes to the words Jesus begins preaching with in Matthew. In the King James Bible: "Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." When Jesus said repent, Luther writes, he meant the whole life of a believer to be repentance. Not one payment: a whole life of turning. Near the end, Luther passes on questions he says ordinary people were asking. One goes, roughly: why does the pope, who is very rich, not build his great church in Rome with his own money instead of the money of poor believers? And here's the surprise. The theses don't yet throw out indulgences. They ask what indulgences can and can't do, and say ordinary people deserve honest answers. Luther also sent them, with a letter, to his archbishop. Then something happened he hadn't planned. Printers got hold of them, translated them out of Latin, and they ran across Germany and beyond far faster than any debate could be arranged. A list meant for scholars became a conversation for everyone. Christians have argued ever since about what that conversation broke and what it opened. But it began as a question.

Let a question come up that you've been carrying but not asking, about faith, work, someone you love or yourself: not an accusation, but a real question you'd like an honest answer to. When it comes, write it down in one sentence, and sit with it there, outside your head. If you pray, bring the question to God as it is.
Ninety-five theses. Luther's numbered claims for debate about indulgences, written in Latin for scholars, and carried by printers to everyone.
Your line: a question for debate. A question can open more than an argument. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Lutheran and other Protestant churches mark Reformation Day at the end of October, remembering the theses; in recent years some Catholic and Lutheran churches have marked it together.

fork.setup: you're Luther. people in your town think a paper letter means they no longer need to change their lives. what do you do?
options: keep quiet; it's above your rank.
write your questions down and invite a debate.
start a new church that week.

chat.says: Did Luther nail the ninety-five theses to a door to start a new church?
options: Historians argue about the hammer. They were Latin claims for debate, not a plan for a new church.
Yes. They were a list of beliefs for a new church, posted for the town to sign.
No. The pope wrote them, and Luther posted them to announce a new indulgence sale.
chat.meaning: A thesis was a claim put up for debate. Luther's asked what indulgences could and couldn't do; then printers carried them everywhere.

notes: Claims rule: the date (31 October 1517) is not stated in the voice; 'on the eve of All Saints' is given inside 'the story goes'. The posting itself is presented as disputed ('historians still argue about the hammer'): the account comes from Melanchthon after Luther's death. Confirm framing. The hook field is reworded from the index.
Thesis 1 and thesis 86 paraphrased. Confirm the paraphrase of 86 (why the pope, whose wealth exceeds the richest, does not build St. Peter's with his own money).
'The theses don't yet throw out indulgences' (cf. thesis 71); confirm.
'People from his own town were coming back with indulgence letters' refers to Wittenberg parishioners who bought from Tetzel across the border; general history, confirm.
Printing and translation into German and spread 'across Germany and beyond' is general history from the index hook; no time or count given.
